newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stock quote bill clears first hurdle in House.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stock quote bill clears first hurdle in House.

text.p: Legislation that would allow stocks on U.S. exchanges to trade in smaller increments by requiring that they be traded in decimals instead of fractions passed its first hurdle in Congress Wednesday.

The bill, which calls on the Securities and Exchange Commission to develop a plan within a year to move stock and options markets away from trading in fractions, was passed on a voice vote by the finance subcommittee of the House Commerce Committee.
The measure must now be considered by the full committee.

"Fractional pricing, whether in intervals of an eighth, a sixteenth, or even small fractions ... still imposes an artifical limit on investors' ability to get better prices through competition," said subcommittee Chairman Michael Oxley, an Ohio Republican who introduced the measure.

Most stocks are traded in eighths or sixteenths of a dollar -- increments of 12.5 cents or 6.25 cents, respectively. Switching to decimals, could in theory, allow these spreads to shrink to as little as 1 cent, supporters of the legislation say.

Despite the potential savings to investors from such a shift, the legislation is opposed by several members on the panel, including all of the members from New York who have echoed the concerns of the securities industry.
"I remain unconvinced that our system needs to be fixed," said Thomas Manton, a Democrat from New York and the ranking minority member on the subcommittee.
Those opposed questioned why lawmakers would force such a shift rather than allowing the markets themselves to make the move.
"We may be facing a scenario where there may be more volatility," said New York Republican Rick Lazio. "I think this is the wrong bill at the wrong time."
Even Michigan Democrat John Dingell, questioned why the panel is moving so rapidly on the measure, which was introduced earlier this year.
"I am curious as to what is the rush here today," Dingell said, adding that the SEC has not been given enough time to study potential implications to the market.
"There will be a significant impact of this legislation on the markets, there also will be an impact on businesses," Dingell warned.
